title: The citywide trend to read every other screen against
question: Year by year, how much does the City pay outside parties, how much of it to nonprofits, how much without competition or approved after the fact, to how many payees, and how concentrated is it?
finding: Outside spending rose from $5.13 billion in fiscal 2019 to $6.90 billion in fiscal 2026 (+34%), while the number of payees went from 5,752 to 5,511 and the 100 largest took 66% and then 61%. Nonprofits received 18% and then 28%. The share keyed under rules that set competition aside was 3.6% in fiscal 2019, peaked at 11.1% in fiscal 2021 and was 9.9% in fiscal 2026; the share keyed as competed went from 57% to 55%. Of contract-type files sent to the Board, 16% were approved after the fact in fiscal 2019 and 8% in fiscal 2026.
how: Outside spending is the part of the Controller’s payment file that buys goods, services, grants and capital work from parties that are not public bodies: $44.69 billion of the $111.39 billion in the file for fiscal 2019 to 2026. Each payment is counted in the fiscal year its voucher was issued, which is read from the voucher number and not from the year the file lists it under. A further $992.6 million of outside spending ($1.08 billion of all payments) that the file lists under those years was issued in fiscal 2018 or earlier; it is in none of the figures here. Left out: fiduciary funds and related bodies such as the retirement and health trusts, as the Controller marks them ($38.09 billion); debt service, benefits, payroll taxes, aid, refunds and other lines that are not purchases or grants ($18.92 billion); taxes and licences, legal judgments, land purchases and housing loans ($5.82 billion); purchases from other public bodies ($3.26 billion); banks, title companies and pooled payee names ($603.4 million). Shares by rule use the purchasing rule keyed on each line; "does not say" covers rules such as "construction services", rent and lines with no rule. Nonprofits are payees the Controller flags as nonprofit on any line; because housing loans and aid passed through nonprofits are left out, the fiscal 2026 figure here, taken as that table takes it by the year the Controller files each line under ($1.96 billion), is below the $2.15 billion in the Controller’s own nonprofit spending table. A payee is new in the first fiscal year any payment to it was issued, looking back to fiscal 2017. The Board column counts contract, agreement, lease and loan files by fiscal year of introduction and the share whose title approves the agreement retroactively.
limits: These are totals, and every one has an ordinary driver: the pandemic emergency of fiscal 2020 to 2022, the ordinances that waived bidding for homelessness and behavioural-health work, and large airport and water-system building programmes that start and finish. The exceptions screens use the whole payment file as their base, so their shares are lower than the ones here. Nonprofit status is the Controller’s flag as of the report date. The rule on a line is whatever staff keyed. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. The $992.6 million of outside spending that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier is in none of the figures here; it is used only to tell that a payee is not new. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
